question.prompt: Before a motorway journey in an electric car, what should you plan?
options: An emergency-area charging stop
Driving until charge is exhausted
Charging only after entering a closed lane
Sufficient charge and suitable recharging opportunities
question.explanation: Rule 97 recommends enough fuel or charge, particularly on motorways. Emergency stopping places are not routine charging stops.

entries.title: A sat nav directs you into a road signed No entry. What should you follow?

question.prompt: A sat nav directs you into a road signed No entry. What should you follow?
options: The traffic sign and a safe alternative route
The shorter sat-nav route
The sat nav if someone follows
Whichever route avoids delay
question.explanation: Traffic signs giving orders must be obeyed. Navigation equipment does not override them.

entries.title: Why deal with unnecessary weight and unsecured items before setting off?

question.prompt: Why deal with unnecessary weight and unsecured items before setting off?
options: They increase the legal speed limit
Load affects handling and loose items can injure occupants
They remove the need for pressure checks
Loose luggage protects people in sudden stops
question.explanation: Stow luggage securely and follow load and tyre-pressure guidance. Items can move violently when the car slows.

entries.title: Severe snow is forecast and your trip can be postponed. What is sensible?

question.prompt: Severe snow is forecast and your trip can be postponed. What is sensible?
options: Leave without checking the route
Drive faster to outrun the weather
Avoid the non-essential journey
Follow any vehicle regardless of conditions
question.explanation: Rule 228 advises against driving in icy or snowy weather unless the journey is essential.

entries.title: Why are tyre-pressure checks part of economical and safe driving?

question.prompt: Why are tyre-pressure checks part of economical and safe driving?
options: Soft tyres make gentle braking unnecessary
One pressure suits every car and load
Only the spare tyre needs checking
Incorrect inflation affects handling, wear and efficient operation
question.explanation: Check cold tyres against manufacturer guidance for the load. Incorrect inflation can harm control and increase unnecessary wear and fuel use.

entries.title: A motorway car develops a problem but can still reach the next service area safely. Where should it stop?

question.prompt: A motorway car develops a problem but can still reach the next service area safely. Where should it stop?
options: In the service area away from moving traffic
In a live lane beside a sign
On the central reservation
At the narrowest hard-shoulder point
question.explanation: A designed parking location offers greater separation from fast traffic. Reach relative safety if possible.

entries.title: You stop on a motorway hard shoulder and can safely leave the car. Where should passengers go?

question.prompt: You stop on a motorway hard shoulder and can safely leave the car. Where should passengers go?
options: Between its rear bumper and traffic
Out on the side away from traffic, then well away from the vehicle
Beside the traffic-side door
Onto the barrier next to the car
question.explanation: If safe and possible, exit furthest from traffic and wait well away, behind a barrier where present while checking for hazards beyond it.

entries.title: Occupants of a car stopped in a motorway live lane cannot leave safely. What should they do?

question.prompt: Occupants of a car stopped in a motorway live lane cannot leave safely. What should they do?
options: Run across the lanes
Stand behind the car to wave traffic away
Keep belts and hazards on and call 999 for police immediately
Try a repair before contacting anyone
question.explanation: If a safe exit away from traffic is not possible, remain belted with hazards on and seek immediate police help.

entries.title: Why must you not place a warning triangle on a motorway?

question.prompt: Why must you not place a warning triangle on a motorway?
options: Triangles are only for fog
It would cancel the hazard lights
Recovery staff are always already present
Placing it would expose you to fast-moving traffic
question.explanation: Never use a warning triangle on a motorway. Do not enter the carriageway to warn traffic or retrieve items.

entries.title: A suitcase falls from your car into a motorway lane. What should you do?

question.prompt: A suitcase falls from your car into a motorway lane. What should you do?
options: Reach relative safety and call emergency services; do not retrieve it
Walk back along the lane
Reverse to shield it
Send a passenger to collect it
question.explanation: Do not remove obstructions yourself from a motorway or other high-speed road. Report them from a place of relative safety.

entries.title: Before rejoining from a motorway emergency area after a breakdown, what must you do?

question.prompt: Before rejoining from a motorway emergency area after a breakdown, what must you do?
options: Follow a passenger’s hand signal alone
Use the emergency telephone and follow the operator’s exit advice
Reverse into the nearest lane
Wait for another broken-down car to follow
question.explanation: Rule 278 requires use of the telephone and compliance with exit advice. A lane closure may be needed.

entries.title: A disability prevents safe exit from a broken-down motorway car. What is advised?

question.prompt: A disability prevents safe exit from a broken-down motorway car. What is advised?
options: Ask a passing driver to lift you into traffic
Walk along the carriageway
Stay belted with hazards on and call 999 for police
Wait without contacting anyone
question.explanation: Rule 279 advises remaining belted, using hazards and seeking police help when normal safe-exit advice cannot be followed.

entries.title: What most helps emergency services locate a motorway breakdown?

question.prompt: What most helps emergency services locate a motorway breakdown?
options: Only the car’s colour
Only the last town passed
Only the intended destination
Road number, direction and nearby location-marker details
question.explanation: Direction of travel and driver-location signs or marker posts help identify the correct carriageway and position.

entries.title: You approach flashing emergency lights around a bend. What should you do?

question.prompt: You approach flashing emergency lights around a bend. What should you do?
options: Slow early, watch for workers and debris and follow directions
Maintain speed until the damaged vehicle appears
Look mainly at the incident
Assume every lane is open
question.explanation: People and obstructions may be in the road before they become visible. Follow police and traffic-officer directions.

entries.title: An incident is on the opposite carriageway. What should you avoid?

question.prompt: An incident is on the opposite carriageway. What should you avoid?
options: Watching your own road
Slowing unnecessarily to stare
Keeping a safe gap
Checking for hazards affecting your lane
question.explanation: Rubbernecking distracts drivers and can create another collision or queue. Stay alert without unnecessary slowing.

entries.title: You are involved in a collision causing injury or property damage. What is the immediate legal requirement?

question.prompt: You are involved in a collision causing injury or property damage. What is the immediate legal requirement?
options: Continue if your own car looks undamaged
Wait until home to leave a message
Stop
Drive away if another person is upset
question.explanation: You must stop after an incident causing the injury or damage covered by Rule 286, then address safety, assistance and required details.

entries.title: Someone reasonably requests your details after a damage collision. What should you provide?

question.prompt: Someone reasonably requests your details after a damage collision. What should you provide?
options: Only a social-media username
Only your garage’s name
Only an estimated repair cost
Name, address, registration and relevant owner details
question.explanation: Rule 286 requires specified identifying details when reasonably requested. Police reporting duties apply if details cannot be given.

entries.title: You cannot provide required details after a collision. When must it be reported to police?

question.prompt: You cannot provide required details after a collision. When must it be reported to police?
options: As soon as reasonably practicable and within 24 hours
At the next insurance renewal
Within a month
Only if the car cannot be driven
question.explanation: Rule 286 requires reporting as soon as reasonably practicable and in any case within 24 hours when details are not given.

entries.title: Why ask people not to smoke at a collision scene?

question.prompt: Why ask people not to smoke at a collision scene?
options: Smoke automatically prevents insurance claims
Fuel or other flammable material may be present
It stops every engine restarting
It replaces calling emergency services
question.explanation: Fire and further collisions are key dangers. Avoid ignition sources and get appropriate help from safety.

entries.title: A goods vehicle with hazardous-material markings has crashed. What is the safe priority?

question.prompt: A goods vehicle with hazardous-material markings has crashed. What is the safe priority?
options: Open the containers
Touch spills to identify them
Keep away and report the markings to emergency services if safely visible
Stand in fumes to direct traffic
question.explanation: Do not handle dangerous substances or take exposure risks. Tell emergency services what can be observed from safety.

entries.title: Where should uninjured people wait after a collision, if they can be moved safely?

question.prompt: Where should uninjured people wait after a collision, if they can be moved safely?
options: Between damaged vehicles
Beside leaking fuel
In the lane emergency vehicles will use
In relative safety away from vehicles and traffic
question.explanation: Move uninjured people away from further impact and other dangers. Injured people should not be moved unless in immediate danger.

entries.title: Before approaching an injured person after a road collision, what comes first?

metadata.reference: Highway Code, Annex 7: Deal with danger

question.prompt: Before approaching an injured person after a road collision, what comes first?
options: Check whether the scene is safe to approach
Check the vehicle’s tax
Ask their intended destination
Take photographs for social media
question.explanation: Check moving traffic, fire, fuel and other dangers. Creating another casualty makes the emergency worse.
question.reference: Highway Code, Annex 7: Deal with danger

entries.title: What casualty information should an emergency caller give?

question.prompt: What casualty information should an emergency caller give?
options: A guessed diagnosis only
Location and observed problems such as entrapment or no response
Only the repair cost
Only which driver seemed at fault
question.explanation: Describe observations such as difficulty breathing, serious bleeding, entrapment or unresponsiveness, and give an accurate location.

entries.title: An injured motorcyclist still has a helmet on. What should an untrained helper normally do?

question.prompt: An injured motorcyclist still has a helmet on. What should an untrained helper normally do?
options: Remove it to help conversation
Twist it loose before checking danger
Leave it in place and follow emergency-service instructions
Use it as a road marker
question.explanation: Do not remove a helmet unless essential; Rule 283 also specifies training. Obtain professional guidance instead of attempting an unfamiliar procedure.

entries.title: An injured occupant is inside a vehicle without immediate danger from its position. What should you normally avoid?

question.prompt: An injured occupant is inside a vehicle without immediate danger from its position. What should you normally avoid?
options: Offering reassurance
Calling for an ambulance
Explaining their position to the operator
Moving them out
question.explanation: Moving a casualty may worsen injury. Do not move injured people unless there is immediate danger.

entries.title: An injured person asks for a drink while awaiting an ambulance. What should you do?

metadata.reference: Highway Code, Annex 7: Help those involved

question.prompt: An injured person asks for a drink while awaiting an ambulance. What should you do?
options: Do not give food or drink; reassure them and follow professional instructions
Offer alcohol to reduce shock
Give a large meal
Give whatever drink is available
question.explanation: Annex 7 advises against giving casualties food or drink. Keep them comfortable and follow the emergency operator.
question.reference: Highway Code, Annex 7: Help those involved

entries.title: How can a bystander help while emergency services are coming?

metadata.reference: Highway Code, Annex 7: Help those involved

question.prompt: How can a bystander help while emergency services are coming?
options: Encourage walking in traffic
Give reassurance and help keep casualties warm and dry without unsafe movement
Leave to look for someone to blame
Promise medical help is unnecessary
question.explanation: Calm reassurance and protection from cold and rain can help. Do not make unsupported medical promises or allow people to wander into traffic.
question.reference: Highway Code, Annex 7: Help those involved

entries.title: A casualty does not respond when spoken to. What should an untrained helper do?

metadata.reference: Highway Code, Annex 7: Get help and emergency care

question.prompt: A casualty does not respond when spoken to. What should an untrained helper do?
options: Assume they are asleep and leave
Give food to wake them
Tell the emergency operator and follow their instructions
Move each limb repeatedly
question.explanation: Unresponsiveness is important information for emergency services. Seek urgent professional guidance; an app is not practical first-aid training.
question.reference: Highway Code, Annex 7: Get help and emergency care

entries.title: Why is reading a first-aid summary different from being trained?

question.prompt: Why is reading a first-aid summary different from being trained?
options: Reading authorises every procedure
Reading removes the need for emergency services
Reading guarantees recovery
Emergencies require practical skills and professional guidance
question.explanation: Annex 7 gives general guidance and recommends proper training. A revision lesson cannot certify practical first-aid competence.

entries.title: Before adding a heavy roof load, what should you check?

question.prompt: Before adding a heavy roof load, what should you check?
options: Vehicle and carrier load limits and how to secure it
Only whether the boot is full
Only the destination’s weather
Only whether the aerial is hidden
question.explanation: Secure the load and do not overload the vehicle or carrier. Follow manufacturer limits and fitting instructions.

entries.title: You add passengers and heavy luggage. Which setting may need adjustment?

question.prompt: You add passengers and heavy luggage. Which setting may need adjustment?
options: The speedometer to read lower
Tyre pressures according to manufacturer guidance for that load
The seat-belt alarm to stay off
The legal tread-depth limit
question.explanation: Tyre pressures must suit the vehicle and load. Use the handbook or vehicle label rather than guessing.

entries.title: Where should heavy items normally be distributed in a caravan or trailer?

question.prompt: Where should heavy items normally be distributed in a caravan or trailer?
options: At the very back
All on one side
Evenly, with heavy items over the axle area within specified limits
Loose near the door
question.explanation: Rule 98 recommends even distribution, heavy items over the axles and the correct tow-ball load. Excess rear weight can contribute to instability.

entries.title: Which statement about towing entitlement is correct?

question.prompt: Which statement about towing entitlement is correct?
options: Any car licence permits every trailer
Only the trailer’s colour matters
A theory pass grants every entitlement
Check that your licence permits the proposed combination
question.explanation: Do not tow more than the licence permits. Check current GOV.UK entitlement and vehicle limits before choosing a combination; do not rely on assumptions about licence dates.

entries.title: Why secure a load even for a short trip?

question.prompt: Why secure a load even for a short trip?
options: It can move during braking or cornering and endanger people
Loads move only on motorways
Short trips suspend load rules
Loose items improve steering
question.explanation: Distance does not remove the risk. Stow and restrain items so normal or emergency driving cannot release them.

entries.title: Before towing, which trailer check is necessary?

question.prompt: Before towing, which trailer check is necessary?
options: Only the paintwork
Its tyres, lights and braking system where fitted
Only that the coupling is near the car
Only the caravan window height
question.explanation: Both the towing vehicle and trailer must be roadworthy. Rule 98 specifically identifies trailer tyres, lights and brakes.

entries.title: How does towing affect decisions about gaps and manoeuvres?

question.prompt: How does towing affect decisions about gaps and manoeuvres?
options: Assume braking is always shorter
Use any gap suitable for the car alone
Allow more time and space for the whole combination
Ignore extra length when turning
question.explanation: Extra length and weight affect manoeuvring, acceleration and braking. Plan for the whole combination.

entries.title: Luggage blocks the view and a loose bag rests on the parcel shelf. What should happen before departure?

question.prompt: Luggage blocks the view and a loose bag rests on the parcel shelf. What should happen before departure?
options: Drive slowly without changing it
Ask passengers to hold it throughout
Remove a mirror for a better forward view
Rearrange and secure the load for adequate vision and control
question.explanation: Secure luggage and maintain the view needed for safe driving. A loose item can become dangerous in a sudden stop.

entries.title: At night, how should speed relate to the road illuminated ahead?

question.prompt: At night, how should speed relate to the road illuminated ahead?
options: Allow stopping within the distance visible to be clear
Match the furthest reflector you notice
Use the maximum regardless of view
Use one fixed speed for dipped headlights
question.explanation: Reduced visibility leaves less distance to deal with an obstruction. Choose a speed that permits stopping within the clear view.

entries.title: What makes a road a dual carriageway for ordinary speed-limit purposes?

question.prompt: What makes a road a dual carriageway for ordinary speed-limit purposes?
options: Two painted lanes each way alone
A central reservation separating opposing directions
Width greater than one car
A 40 mph sign
question.explanation: A central reservation defines a dual carriageway. Lane count alone does not determine the road type.

entries.title: What national limit applies to a normal car without a trailer on a single carriageway?

question.prompt: What national limit applies to a normal car without a trailer on a single carriageway?
options: 70 mph
50 mph
60 mph
40 mph
question.explanation: The national maximum is 60 mph for this vehicle on a single carriageway. Conditions may require a much lower speed.

entries.title: What national motorway limit applies to a car towing a trailer?

question.prompt: What national motorway limit applies to a car towing a trailer?
options: 70 mph
50 mph
40 mph
60 mph
question.explanation: A car towing a trailer has a national motorway maximum of 60 mph. Lower signs and conditions still govern the safe speed.

entries.title: Why should you avoid coasting downhill in neutral?

question.prompt: Why should you avoid coasting downhill in neutral?
options: It removes engine braking and reduces control
It guarantees a tyre will burst
It stops every brake light working
It changes the legal speed limit
question.explanation: Coasting can let speed increase, increase reliance on the footbrake and make selecting the right gear harder.

entries.title: In an emergency stop in an ABS-equipped car, what is the usual advice subject to its handbook?

question.prompt: In an emergency stop in an ABS-equipped car, what is the usual advice subject to its handbook?
options: Pump continuously
Apply the footbrake firmly and maintain pressure until sufficiently slowed
Release whenever ABS operates
Use only the parking brake
question.explanation: Rule 120 advises sustained firm footbrake pressure. ABS helps retain steering control but does not guarantee a shorter stop.

entries.title: A driver follows too closely. What gives you more room to slow gradually if needed?

question.prompt: A driver follows too closely. What gives you more room to slow gradually if needed?
options: Brake sharply in retaliation
Exceed the speed limit
Increase the gap from the vehicle ahead
Keep looking behind instead of ahead
question.explanation: More space ahead reduces dependence on sudden braking. Do not retaliate or speed to escape pressure.

entries.title: Your navigation route needs changing while driving. What should you do?

question.prompt: Your navigation route needs changing while driving. What should you do?
options: Study the screen through the next junction
Ask another driver to hold your lane
Program it while tailgating
Find a safe place to stop before adjusting it
question.explanation: Navigation equipment can distract from observation and control. Make route changes while safely stopped.

entries.title: A bus signals to leave a stop. What should you do when safe?

question.prompt: A bus signals to leave a stop. What should you do when safe?
options: Give it priority and watch for people crossing nearby
Accelerate into the gap
Assume passengers can see through the bus
Sound the horn and maintain speed regardless
question.explanation: Give buses priority when safely possible, especially when leaving stops. People may emerge from behind or ahead of them.

entries.title: A long lorry starts a left turn from away from the kerb. What should you avoid?

question.prompt: A long lorry starts a left turn from away from the kerb. What should you avoid?
options: Waiting at a safe distance
Passing through the gap on its left
Giving it extra room
Preparing to stop
question.explanation: Large vehicles need turning space and may have blind spots beside them. Do not enter a squeeze point.

entries.title: A tall coach blocks your view ahead. What improves your view and planning?

question.prompt: A tall coach blocks your view ahead. What improves your view and planning?
options: Move closer to its bumper
Move across the centre line without a clear view
Drop back to increase separation
Rely only on its brake lights
question.explanation: A larger gap helps you see around the vehicle and react to hazards hidden beyond it.

entries.title: An ambulance approaches while you wait at a red light. What should you do?

question.prompt: An ambulance approaches while you wait at a red light. What should you do?
options: Automatically drive through red
Immediately mount the pavement
Stop watching pedestrians
Make room if safely possible while obeying the signal
question.explanation: Help emergency vehicles without breaking traffic signs or endangering others. Do not panic or make unsafe movements.

entries.title: Your route crosses an approaching tram’s track. What is important to remember?

question.prompt: Your route crosses an approaching tram’s track. What is important to remember?
options: The tram cannot steer around you
It can swerve like a car
It can always stop instantly
Its route follows the nearest car
question.explanation: Trams are confined to tracks and can be quiet. Respect signals and leave space rather than expecting them to swerve.

entries.title: A vehicle ahead has a flashing amber beacon. What should you anticipate?

question.prompt: A vehicle ahead has a flashing amber beacon. What should you anticipate?
options: It invites immediate overtaking
It may be slow, stationary or working
It means the same as a green light
It guarantees an empty road
question.explanation: Amber beacons may mark slow vehicles, road work or incident-support activity. Approach cautiously and assess space.

entries.title: A small mobility vehicle is on the road without a visible amber beacon. What should you do?

question.prompt: A small mobility vehicle is on the road without a visible amber beacon. What should you do?
options: Assume it travels as fast as a car
Pass closely because it is narrow
Allow for low speed and the occupant’s vulnerability
Expect a beacon on every road
question.explanation: Not every mobility vehicle displays a beacon on every road. Its low speed and vulnerable occupant still require patience and room.

entries.title: A large vehicle travels below your car’s permitted speed. What should you consider?

question.prompt: A large vehicle travels below your car’s permitted speed. What should you consider?
options: It must be obstructing deliberately
Your limit forces it to accelerate
Tailgating will improve its visibility
Its legal limit or speed limiter may be lower
question.explanation: Large vehicles can have lower limits or speed limiters. Be patient and overtake only when safe and legal.

entries.title: What visible hazard makes the blue car driver wait behind the cyclist before overtaking?

A car approaching in the opposite direction
A level-crossing barrier

No extra space once the horn is sounded
At least 1.5 metres, and more at higher speeds

entries.title: Being fit to drive

lesson.title: Being fit to drive
objectives: Recognise when health, tiredness or substances make driving unsafe.
Plan a safe response before the journey starts.

sections.title: Start with the driver
paragraphs: A safe car cannot compensate for a driver who cannot concentrate or control it. Assess your sleep, vision, health and medicines before collecting the keys. Feeling determined to finish a journey is not evidence of fitness. A heavy meal, a warm cabin and a monotonous road can make tiredness harder to recognise. Plan a realistic journey rather than treating rest as something to earn after arrival. If you are already tired, postpone the drive or arrange another driver.

sections.title: Know the legal duties
paragraphs: You MUST meet the eyesight requirement and wear glasses or contact lenses while driving if you need them to meet it. You MUST report to DVLA a health condition likely to affect driving. You MUST NOT drive while impaired by alcohol, drugs or medicines. Scotland has lower legal alcohol limits than England and Wales; counting drinks is not a reliable test of safety. Alcohol can still impair you the next morning, and coffee does not remove it from your body.

sections.title: Manage the journey
paragraphs: The Highway Code recommends a break of at least 15 minutes after every two hours of driving. That is planning advice, not permission to continue until two hours have passed when you become sleepy sooner. Stop somewhere suitable, such as a service area or designated parking place. A hard shoulder or emergency area is not a rest stop. Ask a pharmacist or doctor about a medicine that may affect driving; a legal prescription does not make impaired driving safe.
At night or in poor visibility, do not use tinted glasses, lenses or visors if they restrict your vision.

scenario.title: Put it into practice
scenario.text: You slept poorly and are due to drive for several hours. Before leaving, you arrange a later departure and a rested driver rather than relying on an open window. If sleepiness develops on the road, you look for a safe stopping place instead of pushing on to the planned break.

takeaways: Decide fitness before moving.
Treat sleepiness as a reason to stop safely.
Follow eyesight, medical-reporting and impairment requirements.

entries.title: Licence, insurance and legal readiness

lesson.title: Licence, insurance and legal readiness
objectives: Check that the driver and vehicle are legally ready for the trip.
Distinguish a certificate from ongoing roadworthiness.

sections.title: Permission belongs to this journey
paragraphs: Before driving, confirm that your licence covers the vehicle category and that valid insurance covers your use of that vehicle. A friend owning an insured car does not automatically make you an insured borrower. Ask about restrictions instead of assuming that comprehensive cover allows every person to drive every car. You MUST hold the appropriate valid licence and insurance. Keep your licence details up to date and notify DVLA when your name or address changes.

sections.title: The vehicle must remain roadworthy
paragraphs: An ordinary car normally needs its first MOT after three years and then annually, with exceptions for some vehicles. Check the current requirement for the particular vehicle rather than memorising an exception as a general rule. A valid MOT is a record of a test, not a promise that a tyre, light or brake cannot subsequently become defective. The car must be legal and roadworthy whenever used. Tax or an applicable exemption, registration duties and insurance are separate responsibilities.

sections.title: Learning has conditions
paragraphs: A car learner needs a valid provisional licence and an eligible supervisor. For ordinary private supervision, the supervisor must be at least 21 and have held the suitable full licence for at least three years. Learner plates must be clearly displayed front and rear; red D plates are an alternative in Wales. A theory pass alone does not allow unsupervised driving. Motorway learning has additional instructor and dual-control requirements. If police request documents, comply with the production instructions, including the seven-day arrangement when applicable.
For road use, the legal minimum is third-party insurance covering your use of the vehicle for injury or damage caused to others; an MOT certificate or breakdown membership is not insurance.

scenario.title: Put it into practice
scenario.text: A relative offers their spare car for an afternoon lesson. You check your provisional entitlement, the supervisor’s eligibility, learner plates and insurance for your use. Although its MOT is current, a damaged tyre means the lesson waits until the car is roadworthy. No single document replaces the other checks.

takeaways: Check licence and insurance for the specific use.
Treat MOT, roadworthiness and tax as separate checks.
A theory pass does not remove supervision requirements.

entries.title: Observation, attitude and developing hazards

lesson.title: Observation, attitude and developing hazards
objectives: Turn visible clues into a plan before danger develops.
Respond calmly to uncertainty and other people’s mistakes.

sections.title: Look for what could happen
paragraphs: Observation is more than spotting objects directly ahead. Scan the distance, the middle of your route and the space nearby, while checking mirrors often enough to understand what is beside and behind you. Parked vehicles can hide a child, a junction can hide a cyclist, and a bus can hide a crossing pedestrian. Ask what could enter your path and what space you would need to respond. A potential hazard becomes urgent when it starts affecting your intended route.

sections.title: Check before changing your plan
paragraphs: Use mirrors before changing speed or direction and check the relevant blind spot when necessary. Before moving off, make an all-round final check and move only when safe. Another person’s indicator may have been left on, while a headlight flash only draws attention to the vehicle’s presence. Neither grants you priority. Reduce uncertainty by waiting for a clear view and a genuinely safe gap, rather than substituting an assumed signal for observation.

sections.title: Keep a useful attitude
paragraphs: Pressure and anger encourage rushed decisions. If someone tailgates or behaves aggressively, keep your own driving calm, avoid retaliation and preserve space ahead. Never try to teach another driver a lesson by blocking or braking sharply. Some people cannot see or hear your approach, so do not assume a horn or eye contact guarantees a response. Put phones and distractions aside before moving; waiting at a red light is still part of driving, not a routine opportunity to handle a phone.
Choose a speed that lets you stop well within the distance you can see to be clear; a posted limit does not guarantee that distance is available.

scenario.title: Put it into practice
scenario.text: A ball rolls from behind a parked van while a driver behind is close to your bumper. You ease your speed early and create time to stop for a possible child. You do not wait for a child to emerge, and you do not accelerate to satisfy the following driver. The clue, not the pressure, controls your plan.

takeaways: Look for hidden people as well as visible vehicles.
A signal does not guarantee another person’s action.
Create time and space instead of reacting with anger.

entries.title: Planning a considerate, efficient journey

lesson.title: Planning a considerate, efficient journey
objectives: Prepare route, breaks, fuel or charge before setting off.
Use economical habits that also preserve control.

sections.title: Remove pressure before departure
paragraphs: Check the route, traffic and weather, then allow enough time for delays and breaks. Know where the controls are before entering traffic and set navigation while safely parked. A long journey needs enough fuel or charge and realistic places to replenish it; motorway emergency areas are not routine refuelling or charging stops. Consider postponing a non-essential journey during severe snow or ice. Changing the plan before departure is often safer than trying to solve a foreseeable problem at speed.

sections.title: Drive smoothly without losing control
paragraphs: Looking ahead lets you ease off early rather than alternate hard acceleration with late braking. Keep a safe following gap so that minor speed changes ahead do not force sudden reactions. Check cold tyre pressures against the manufacturer’s guidance for the load, and avoid carrying unnecessary weight. These habits support efficient operation as well as control. Do not coast in neutral or hold the clutch down to save fuel: removing engine braking can make downhill speed and vehicle control harder to manage.

sections.title: Respect people and the environment
paragraphs: You MUST NOT leave an unattended parked vehicle with its engine running or run it unnecessarily while stationary on a public road. Rule 123 distinguishes unnecessary idling from waiting in traffic or diagnosing a fault. For a longer parked wait, switching off reduces noise and emissions. Keep exhaust and other vehicle systems maintained. Secure luggage and charging cables so that an efficient trip does not create hazards for passengers or pedestrians. Avoid changing navigation equipment while driving; stop somewhere safe first.
Satnav directions never override signs, restrictions or the conditions you can see. If a direction conflicts with a No entry sign, obey the sign and find a lawful route.

scenario.title: Put it into practice
scenario.text: You plan an unfamiliar motorway trip in an electric car. You choose a charging stop with reserve charge, build in a break and set the route before moving. During a delay, you keep a safe gap and adjust the arrival plan instead of speeding later. At the destination, you park close enough to the charger to avoid a trailing cable across the walkway.

takeaways: Plan for delays, rest and fuel or charge.
Smooth driving is different from coasting.
Avoid unnecessary parked idling and unsecured loads.

entries.title: Controls, visibility and restraints

lesson.title: Controls, visibility and restraints
objectives: Prepare a driving position that gives control and a clear view.
Protect occupants with suitable restraints and secure luggage.

sections.title: Set up before moving
paragraphs: In an unfamiliar car, find the lights, indicators, wipers, demisters and hazard switch while parked. Adjust the seat so that you can operate the pedals and steering comfortably without stretching. Position mirrors to give the best available view, while remembering that blind spots remain. Adjust the head restraint correctly to reduce injury risk. Clean and demist windows and mirrors; a small clear patch is not adequate observation. Footwear and clothing should allow proper control throughout the journey.

sections.title: Use protection correctly
paragraphs: You MUST use seat belts where required, even on a short journey. Children need the restraint appropriate to the legal requirements and to their size, with fitting instructions followed carefully. A rear-facing baby seat MUST NOT be used in a seat protected by an active frontal airbag. Check the vehicle and restraint instructions rather than improvising a fitting. A loose or twisted belt, an unsuitable seat or an incorrect installation may leave someone poorly protected even though a restraint is present.

sections.title: Keep the cabin safe
paragraphs: Stow luggage securely so it cannot move into people or controls during a sharp stop. Keep the driver’s view and mirrors usable, and do not let a phone or navigation mount obstruct essential vision. Passengers, particularly children, should normally leave on the kerb side when safe. Before opening a door, look all around for cyclists and other passing people. Preparing the cabin is part of driving responsibility, not a task to finish while pulling away from the kerb.

scenario.title: Put it into practice
scenario.text: Before driving a borrowed car, you adjust the seat and mirrors, find the demister and fit a child restraint according to its instructions. A bag on the rear shelf is moved into secure storage. You check the child can leave safely on arrival instead of waiting until traffic is passing the open door.

takeaways: Adjust controls and visibility while parked.
Use and fit restraints correctly for every trip.
Secure loose items and check before opening doors.

entries.title: Tyres, brakes, lights and fluids

lesson.title: Tyres, brakes, lights and fluids
objectives: Recognise checks that support roadworthiness.
Respond to a defect without relying on an old certificate.

sections.title: Use a regular checking routine
paragraphs: Take time to inspect tyres, lights, windows and the area around the car before a journey. The car and any trailer MUST be roadworthy. Check that lights, indicators, brakes, steering, wipers, washers and demisters operate, and keep lights, number plates and windows clean and unobstructed. A current MOT does not cancel this responsibility. A defect that appears between tests still needs attention; discovering it early is preferable to finding it while joining fast traffic or approaching a crossing.

sections.title: Understand the contact with the road
paragraphs: For ordinary cars, tyres MUST have at least 1.6 millimetres of tread across the central three-quarters and around the entire circumference. They must be inflated to the manufacturer’s specification for the load. Check pressures when cold, because heat can make readings misleading. Look for damage and uneven wear as well as depth. A car pulling to one side while braking may have a fault that needs professional attention. Do not use one symptom as proof that a journey is safe to continue.

sections.title: Check fluids without creating danger
paragraphs: Follow the handbook for oil, coolant, brake-fluid and washer checks, including the correct level marks and vehicle conditions. Do not open a hot coolant filler cap: heat and pressure can cause serious injury. Low brake fluid or a persistent warning can indicate a serious problem rather than a simple need to top up. If a check is unfamiliar or a defect affects safety, obtain competent assistance. Keep the vehicle out of use until the fault has been assessed and made safe.

scenario.title: Put it into practice
scenario.text: You notice low tread on one tyre and a brake warning after start-up. Instead of relying on last month’s MOT, you arrange inspection and alternative transport. The next day, with the car cool and safely parked, you use the handbook to check the recommended pressures and fluid levels rather than guessing from another vehicle.

takeaways: MOT validity does not guarantee present roadworthiness.
Check tyre depth, damage and cold pressures.
Use the handbook and treat brake or overheating faults seriously.

entries.title: Carrying loads and towing safely

lesson.title: Carrying loads and towing safely
objectives: Check limits, secure loads and maintain visibility.
Allow for a trailer’s extra weight and length.

sections.title: Plan for the entire load
paragraphs: Adding people, luggage or a roof carrier changes the vehicle, even before a trailer is attached. You MUST NOT overload the car or trailer, and you must remain within licence entitlement and vehicle limits. Check current towing entitlement and the manufacturer’s figures for the proposed combination rather than relying on a friend’s licence or an old rule about test dates. Roof carriers have their own fitting and load limits. Make these checks before accepting a load, not after reaching the roadside.

sections.title: Distribute and secure it
paragraphs: Heavy items in a caravan or trailer should be distributed evenly around the axle area, within the specified overall and tow-ball limits. Too much weight at the rear can encourage instability. Secure items against braking, cornering and movement; passengers holding a loose bag is not reliable restraint. Keep adequate vision through mirrors, fitting suitable towing mirrors if the trailer blocks the required rear view. Adjust tyre pressures for the load using the vehicle’s instructions, and check trailer tyres, brakes and lights.

sections.title: Drive as a combination
paragraphs: Allow more time and room to accelerate, brake, turn and pass other road users. A gap that fits a solo car may be too short for a towing combination. Trailer speed limits and motorway lane restrictions differ from those for a solo car, so check the relevant rules and signs. If the combination becomes unstable, do not assume that driving faster will cure it. Stop safely and have loading, equipment or other causes assessed before continuing. Loading is part of safe control, not merely a storage problem.

scenario.title: Put it into practice
scenario.text: A holiday trailer hides your normal rear view and most of the luggage is piled behind its axle. You check entitlement and vehicle limits, redistribute and secure the load and fit appropriate mirrors before departure. On the road you select a larger gap and earlier braking points for the combination, rather than driving as though the trailer were not attached.

takeaways: Check entitlement and manufacturer limits.
Distribute weight, secure it and preserve the required view.
Use combination-appropriate gaps, speeds and lane choices.

entries.title: Warnings that need prompt action

lesson.title: Warnings that need prompt action
objectives: Distinguish a start-up check from a warning during a journey.
Choose a safe stopping response rather than a guessed repair.

sections.title: Read the warning in context
paragraphs: Many lamps illuminate briefly when the car performs its start-up check. A light that remains on, returns while driving or appears with a message may mean something different. Learn the controls and warning displays in the vehicle’s handbook before departure. Colour is a useful attention cue, but it is not a diagnosis: a symbol, accompanying message and the manufacturer’s instructions determine the response. The same general symbol can have different details in different cars, so avoid relying on a photograph alone.

sections.title: Protect people before investigating
paragraphs: A red oil-pressure or temperature warning can signal a problem that makes continued running damaging or unsafe. A red brake warning that remains after the parking brake is released requires serious attention. Reduce speed in a controlled way and find a safe place to stop, following the vehicle’s instructions. Do not stop abruptly in a live lane merely to look at the dashboard when a safer stopping place is reachable. If the car cannot reach relative safety, use the breakdown procedure and call for appropriate help.

sections.title: Do not confuse a check with a repair
paragraphs: A charging warning may mean the electrical system is not charging, rather than simply identifying a flat battery. A low fluid warning may reflect a leak or other fault. Repeatedly restarting, ignoring a warning because the car still moves, or topping up without understanding the fault can make matters worse. Do not remove a hot coolant cap. Arrange competent assessment and use the handbook’s instructions for that exact vehicle. Roadside revision cannot replace professional diagnosis or a safe repair.

scenario.title: Put it into practice
scenario.text: A red temperature symbol appears during a journey. You keep control, find a suitable safe stopping place and follow the handbook rather than continuing to the destination. You do not open the hot cooling system. If stopping leaves you exposed to high-speed traffic, protecting the occupants and getting help takes priority over examining the engine.

takeaways: Read the symbol, message and handbook together.
Stop safely for serious warnings; avoid abrupt unsafe stops.
A lamp identifies a concern, not a complete diagnosis.

entries.title: System warnings and normal indicators

lesson.title: System warnings and normal indicators
objectives: Recognise common safety-system alerts and operating indicators.
Use a persistent warning to guide a safe next action.

sections.title: Notice when a system is reporting trouble
paragraphs: Amber ABS, engine-management, tyre-pressure or restraint-system warnings commonly draw attention to a system that needs checking. The exact response depends on the vehicle, whether the lamp is steady or flashing, and any other warning or change in behaviour. A car appearing to drive normally does not prove that every safety system is available. Read the message and handbook, adjust the journey if required and seek competent advice. Never remove a warning lamp’s power or cover it to avoid the concern.

sections.title: Separate intervention from a persistent fault
paragraphs: A traction or stability symbol may flash while a system responds to reduced grip, whereas a persistent warning can indicate a fault or a disabled function. Neither is permission to drive beyond the conditions. If tyres are losing grip, make your own inputs smoother and increase space instead of relying on electronics to solve the problem. A tyre-pressure alert calls for a safe opportunity to assess the tyres according to instructions, not an attempt to investigate while moving in traffic.

sections.title: Recognise reminders and status
paragraphs: Not every illuminated symbol is a fault. A seat-belt reminder means occupants and restraints need attention before continuing. A low-fuel indication should prompt a sensible refuelling plan before the car becomes stranded. A blue main-beam indicator shows a lighting mode; dip the headlights when necessary to avoid dazzling others. These examples teach a method: identify what is active, connect it with the driving situation, then take the appropriate action. Do not memorise one colour as meaning that every journey may continue unchanged.

scenario.title: Put it into practice
scenario.text: On a wet bend the stability symbol flashes briefly, so you ease your inputs and allow more room. Later, an amber symbol stays on during ordinary driving. You treat that as a different situation, find a safe place to read the message and handbook, and arrange a check rather than assuming it is still a normal intervention.

takeaways: A flashing intervention and a persistent warning may differ.
Driver assistance does not create grip or remove responsibility.
Know normal indicators as well as fault warnings.

entries.title: Signals, lights and clear communication

lesson.title: Signals, lights and clear communication
objectives: Give signals that inform without misleading.
Use lights and warnings for their proper purpose.

sections.title: Communicate a plan, not a demand
paragraphs: Check mirrors and the situation around you before signalling a change of direction or position. Signal early enough to help others, but not so early that a different turn appears intended. If you plan to turn just beyond a side road, an early indicator may persuade someone at that side road to emerge. Cancel the signal after use. A signal explains your intention; it does not give priority or make a manoeuvre safe. Continue observing while the manoeuvre develops.

sections.title: Interpret other people cautiously
paragraphs: Another vehicle’s indicator may have been left on. A headlight flash is a warning of that vehicle’s presence, not a promise that the driver will wait or that every other lane is clear. Never transfer responsibility for a decision to an assumed invitation. You MUST obey traffic lights, signs giving orders and directions from authorised people. Temporary controls at road works deserve the same attention as permanent controls. Wait for a clear view and a safe situation rather than guessing from someone else’s signal.

sections.title: Use warnings without creating another hazard
paragraphs: Use headlights at night when required and avoid dazzling other road users. You MUST use headlights when visibility is seriously reduced; front or rear fog lights may be used in such conditions, but MUST be switched off when visibility improves. Use the horn as a warning of presence, not to express impatience. Hazard lights have specific warning uses: they do not authorise illegal parking or excuse poor lane discipline. Learn the controls while parked so that searching for a switch does not distract you from the road.

scenario.title: Put it into practice
scenario.text: You intend to turn left immediately after a side street. You check behind and delay the indicator until it will no longer suggest the first turn. A driver at the junction flashes headlights. You continue to assess the road yourself rather than assuming the flash guarantees a safe path or changes the traffic lights.

takeaways: Time signals so they are useful and unambiguous.
A flash or indicator is not a guarantee of another person’s action.
Use lights and warnings correctly, including switching fog lights off again.

entries.title: Choosing speed, space and control

lesson.title: Choosing speed, space and control
objectives: Distinguish a maximum speed from a safe speed.
Create time to stop and use smooth, effective control.

sections.title: Choose a speed for the view
paragraphs: A speed limit is a maximum, not a target. You MUST NOT exceed the limit for the road or vehicle, but bends, parked cars, pedestrians, weather and restricted views may require much less. For ordinary cars without trailers, national limits are 60 mph on single carriageways and 70 mph on dual carriageways and motorways. Different vehicle types and towing combinations have different limits. Street-lit roads generally have a 30 mph limit in England and Scotland and 20 mph in Wales, unless signs show otherwise.

sections.title: Make space work for you
paragraphs: Drive at a speed that allows you to stop within the distance visible to be clear. On high-speed roads in dry conditions, the Highway Code advises at least a two-second following gap. Choose a fixed roadside point and compare when each vehicle passes it. Wet conditions require at least double the normal gap; poor grip or visibility may need considerably more. A larger gap also improves the view beyond a tall vehicle. If someone follows you too closely, increase space ahead so you can slow progressively rather than retaliating.

sections.title: Keep control while slowing
paragraphs: Look well ahead and brake in good time with smooth inputs for ordinary slowing. An emergency may require immediate firm braking. With ABS, follow the handbook; the usual emergency advice is firm footbrake pressure held until sufficiently slowed, not pumping the pedal. ABS helps steering control but does not guarantee a shorter stop. Avoid coasting in neutral or with the clutch held down, because it removes engine braking and can reduce control. Harsh steering, braking or acceleration can exceed available grip and cause a skid.

scenario.title: Put it into practice
scenario.text: On a dark road with a national limit, your headlights reveal a bend well before its exit becomes visible. You slow below the limit so you can stop within your clear view. Rain begins, so you increase the gap to the car ahead. You keep a suitable gear rather than coasting downhill toward the bend.

takeaways: Use the lower of the legal maximum and the speed conditions allow.
Measure a useful time gap and increase it when conditions worsen.
Smooth ordinary control and effective emergency braking are different skills.

entries.title: Reading markings and the road layout

lesson.title: Reading markings and the road layout
objectives: Use lines, studs and physical layout as early information.
Check the road type without relying on lane count or navigation.

sections.title: Read the road before reaching a hazard
paragraphs: Painted lines and lane arrows help explain the road ahead, often before the hazard itself is visible. A broken centre line whose markings grow longer and gaps shorter warns of a hazard ahead. Start checking your speed, view and position instead of treating it as decoration. Lane arrows and destination markings help you choose a lane early. Do not make a sudden move simply because a navigation instruction arrived late; a missed turn is safer to correct by a new route.

sections.title: Understand separation and restrictions
paragraphs: A dual carriageway has a central reservation separating opposing traffic; two lanes in each direction without that separation are not enough to make it one. This matters when interpreting national limits, but the maximum still depends on the vehicle and any lower signs. Different centre-line arrangements carry different overtaking and crossing restrictions. Read them together with signs and your view rather than assuming that every long straight road permits a pass. Never use a clear marking as a substitute for checking people and traffic.

sections.title: Use night-time clues carefully
paragraphs: Reflective studs help show the road’s shape and boundaries in darkness. Amber studs mark the central-reservation edge of a motorway or dual carriageway. Other colours identify different edges and lane features; learn their meaning rather than following the lights of the vehicle ahead. Wet surfaces, glare and road works may make markings harder to interpret. Reduce speed when information is unclear, follow temporary layouts and keep a stopping margin. A familiar route can change, so continue looking for current signs and markings on every journey.

scenario.title: Put it into practice
scenario.text: An unfamiliar road has two lanes each way but no central reservation. You do not assume it has the same national limit as a dual carriageway. Farther ahead, longer broken centre markings warn of a hazard. You ease speed and inspect the view before considering any lane change, despite the sat nav asking for a turn.

takeaways: Read markings as early clues to hazards and lane choice.
A central reservation, not lane count, defines a dual carriageway.
Use studs and markings alongside signs, visibility and observation.

entries.title: The language of traffic signs

lesson.title: The language of traffic signs
objectives: Recognise the main sign families before reading their detail.
Connect shape, colour and symbol with the required driving decision.

sections.title: Start with the sign family
paragraphs: Traffic signs use a visual language so that a driver can recognise a function quickly. Circles usually give orders, upright triangles usually warn and rectangles usually provide information. Colour adds meaning: a red ring normally restricts an action, while a blue circle generally gives a positive instruction or identifies a route for particular road users. These are useful starting clues, not a licence to guess an unfamiliar symbol. Look at the whole sign, including any text or additional plate, before deciding what it means.

sections.title: Learn the important exceptions
paragraphs: The eight-sided STOP sign and the inverted GIVE WAY triangle stand out from the usual families. Their shapes help recognition even before lettering is read. A red-bordered speed sign states a maximum, while the national-speed-limit sign directs you to the limit for that road and vehicle class; it is not one universal number. A blue circular arrow differs from a triangular warning showing a bend: one gives an instruction, while the other alerts you to a change or danger ahead.

sections.title: Turn recognition into a safe action
paragraphs: Reading a sign correctly is only the first step. Ask what it requires you to change: stop, give way, choose a permitted route, reduce speed for a hazard or plan an exit. You MUST obey signs giving orders. Warnings and information still need an appropriate response, even though their purpose differs. A sign does not remove the need to observe people, traffic and surface conditions. Practise recognising the symbol and explaining the action in your own words, rather than remembering only a colour or an answer letter.

scenario.title: Put it into practice
scenario.text: You see an upright red triangle before a bend and later a blue circle with a left arrow on a traffic island. For the first, you inspect the bend and adjust speed to the conditions. For the second, you plan to pass the island on the instructed side. Recognising the families prevents you treating both arrows as the same type of message.

takeaways: Use shape and colour as clues, then read the symbol and plates.
Learn STOP and GIVE WAY as distinctive exceptions.
Explain the driving action, not just the sign’s name.

entries.title: Orders, restrictions and speed limits

lesson.title: Orders, restrictions and speed limits
objectives: Apply common regulatory signs without confusing similar symbols.
Check restrictions against the vehicle, route and additional plates.

sections.title: Read exactly what is restricted
paragraphs: Red-bordered signs can prohibit entry, a turn, overtaking or a class of vehicle. The familiar No entry sign has a horizontal white bar on red; the car-and-motorcycle symbol means No motor vehicles. Do not substitute one meaning for the other just because both prevent some traffic proceeding. Supplementary plates may define times, exceptions or other details. Read them when deciding whether a restriction applies to you, and choose a safe alternative if the road is not available.

sections.title: Respect instructions and limits
paragraphs: A blue circular arrow may require a direction or the side on which to pass an obstruction. STOP requires a complete stop before crossing the stop line, followed by a proper check before entering the major road. GIVE WAY requires priority to traffic on the major road; stop if that is necessary to give way safely. Height, width and weight restrictions must be considered before reaching a narrowing or bridge. Know the relevant dimensions and limits of the vehicle and load rather than relying on the vehicle ahead.

sections.title: Keep maximum and suitable speed separate
paragraphs: A red-ring speed sign sets a maximum in miles per hour, if it is safe to travel that fast. Larger terminal signs mark a change; smaller repeaters may remind you of a limit where provided. A 20 mph zone can include traffic-calming features, so continue looking for road humps, pedestrians and narrowings. A national-limit sign means the appropriate limit for your vehicle and road type. Even with no other traffic visible, a signed maximum does not promise that the next bend or weather condition is safe at that speed.

scenario.title: Put it into practice
scenario.text: You approach an unfamiliar street and notice a red restriction sign with a supplementary plate. Instead of following a van through, you check whether your own vehicle is permitted and use another route if not. At a later STOP sign you stop at the line, check both the main road and the area you will enter, and move only when safe.

takeaways: Similar shapes can carry different restrictions.
Read plates and know the relevant vehicle or load limits.
Obey maximum speeds and choose a lower speed when needed.

entries.title: Warnings, information and route planning

lesson.title: Warnings, information and route planning
objectives: Use warning signs to plan before reaching the hazard.
Read direction information early without making sudden manoeuvres.

sections.title: Prepare for the hazard ahead
paragraphs: An upright red-bordered triangle warns rather than grants priority. Its symbol tells you what to look for: a bend, narrowing, junction, pedestrian activity, slippery surface or another feature. Reduce speed and choose a position that leaves time and room to respond. A bend symbol does not tell you an exact safe speed or guarantee a clear road beyond it. A steep-descent warning is a cue to plan speed and a suitable gear early, not to wait until the car is gathering speed downhill.

sections.title: Read the supporting information
paragraphs: A plate can show distance to a hazard or explain the warning. A junction diagram may indicate the road arrangement, but it cannot show every road user arriving now. A crossing warning asks you to search for people and prepare to stop; it is different from the traffic control at the crossing itself. Pay attention to signs for level crossings and water or quay edges. If information is unclear, slow sufficiently to investigate from safety rather than committing to a manoeuvre you cannot complete.

sections.title: Plan the route without being trapped by it
paragraphs: Direction-sign backgrounds help identify the route network: motorway direction signs use blue, primary-route directions green and non-primary directions white. Other information signs have their own purposes, including parking, a no-through road or a change in road layout. Read destinations and lane information early, then use mirrors and signals for any necessary move. A sign or sat nav may help choose the route, but neither justifies a sharp cut across another lane. If you miss the turn, continue safely and find another route.

scenario.title: Put it into practice
scenario.text: A warning sign shows a double bend before a direction sign for your destination. You slow for the limited view and read the lane information early. A following vehicle occupies the lane you would need, so you continue on the safe route instead of cutting across it. The direction sign helps planning; it does not make your chosen exit compulsory at any cost.

takeaways: Warnings are cues for observation and early adjustment.
Read plates and assess the actual hazard, not only the picture.
Missing a turn is preferable to a sudden unsafe lane change.

entries.title: Approaching junctions and giving way

lesson.title: Approaching junctions and giving way
objectives: Identify the control and make a safe observation plan.
Choose a gap that fits the whole manoeuvre and vehicle.

sections.title: Prepare before the line
paragraphs: Read signs and markings early, check mirrors and adjust speed so you can assess the junction without rushing. Look for pedestrians, cyclists and motorcycles as well as larger vehicles. Buildings, hedges, parked cars and a large turning vehicle can hide another road user. An indicator on an approaching car may be incorrect or left on. Wait until the situation is genuinely clear rather than treating the signal, a headlight flash or another person’s wave as permission to emerge.

sections.title: Respect STOP and GIVE WAY
paragraphs: At a STOP sign with its solid stop line, you MUST come to a complete stop before crossing the line. Then check carefully and move only when the way is clear. At a Give Way line you MUST give way to traffic on the major road; stopping may be needed, but the sign does not itself demand a fixed pause of a particular number of seconds. A large vehicle turning into your road may need extra space. Keep back and wait rather than trying to squeeze alongside its turning path.

sections.title: Check the space beyond the first gap
paragraphs: A safe gap must last long enough for your whole vehicle to complete the move without forcing another road user to alter course or speed. When crossing or turning right at a dual carriageway, assess the central reservation. If it is wide enough to hold the entire vehicle safely, the manoeuvre may be treated in stages. If it cannot hold the whole vehicle, wait for a safe opportunity to complete the full crossing. Include the length of any trailer, not merely the car, when assessing the space.

scenario.title: Put it into practice
scenario.text: You intend to emerge from a side road while a lorry turns into it. The lorry blocks your view of a motorcycle beyond it and uses much of the entrance. You stay behind the line until it has passed and your view is clear. You then select a gap for the whole manoeuvre instead of following the lorry’s signal.

takeaways: Stop fully where required and give way to the main-road traffic.
Look for people hidden by vehicles or the roadside.
Assess a central reservation against the whole vehicle’s length.

entries.title: Turning while protecting other road users

lesson.title: Turning while protecting other road users
objectives: Plan position, observation and signals before a turn.
Give pedestrians and cyclists the room and priority they need.

sections.title: Plan the path before turning
paragraphs: Use mirrors, a clear signal and an appropriate position so others can understand your intention. A right turn from an ordinary two-way road normally starts near the centre of the road without cutting the corner. A left turn should not sweep across someone travelling alongside. Slow enough to make the final observations properly, and check the road you will enter as well as the road you are leaving. Signalling does not remove the responsibility to make a safe turn.

sections.title: Look where someone could be hidden
paragraphs: Cyclists and motorcyclists may approach alongside slow traffic or be obscured by another vehicle. Look for them again before completing a right turn. Do not turn across a cyclist going straight ahead if that would make the cyclist stop or swerve. A cycle track can carry cyclists approaching from either direction, so check both ways before crossing it. Avoid overtaking a cyclist just before a left turn and then cutting across their route. Leave space and wait behind instead when necessary.

sections.title: Include pedestrians in the decision
paragraphs: At a junction, you should give way to pedestrians crossing or waiting to cross the road into or from which you are turning. This includes the entrance or exit of the road, not only a marked pedestrian crossing. Slow sufficiently to recognise people waiting near the kerb and allow time for older or disabled people to cross. Do not hurry them with the vehicle or a horn. Priority is guidance for preventing conflict, not a reason to force your way through an unsafe situation.

scenario.title: Put it into practice
scenario.text: You signal left into a side street. A cyclist continues straight along the road on your left, and a pedestrian waits at the side street’s mouth. You remain behind the cyclist rather than overtaking and cutting across. You give the pedestrian time to cross and turn only after checking that both the route and the receiving road are clear.

takeaways: Observe both roads and the full path of the turn.
Do not cut across a cyclist continuing ahead.
Give way to pedestrians crossing or waiting at the junction.

entries.title: Traffic lights, box junctions and waiting areas

lesson.title: Traffic lights, box junctions and waiting areas
objectives: Respond to lights without entering a space you cannot clear.
Apply the box-junction exception accurately.

sections.title: Understand the traffic signal
paragraphs: You MUST stop at red. Amber also means stop unless you have already crossed the stop line or are so close that stopping might cause a collision. Do not accelerate merely to beat a changing light. A green signal means you may proceed if the way is clear; it does not authorise blocking the junction or taking priority over someone still crossing. A green filter arrow permits the indicated direction when appropriate, while you continue to check the path and other road users.

sections.title: Check the exit before entering
paragraphs: You MUST NOT enter a yellow box junction until your exit road or lane is clear. There is a specific exception when turning right and prevented only by oncoming traffic or other vehicles waiting to turn right. Do not stretch that exception to cover a stationary queue blocking the road you want to enter. Look beyond the first car and allow room for your whole vehicle. A following driver’s impatience or a green light does not make a blocked exit acceptable.

sections.title: Respect waiting areas and uncertainty
paragraphs: At lights with an advanced cyclist waiting area, a driver must normally stop at the first stop line and leave the marked area for cyclists. Do not use it to gain a better position in the queue. Keep watching for people on both sides of the road as the signal changes. If traffic lights fail, treat the junction with great caution, assess the other traffic and proceed only when safe. Do not assume that your usual green phase or main-road status makes the failed signals harmless.

scenario.title: Put it into practice
scenario.text: Your signal turns green, but the queue beyond the yellow box has not moved far enough to fit your car. You wait before the box. Later, when turning right, the exit is clear but oncoming vehicles prevent completion; that is the different situation covered by the right-turn exception. You keep checking pedestrians and cyclists while waiting.

takeaways: Green does not mean enter a blocked junction.
Use the right-turn box exception only in its stated situation.
Leave cyclist waiting areas clear and treat failed signals cautiously.

entries.title: Approaching a roundabout with a plan

lesson.title: Approaching a roundabout with a plan
objectives: Choose an approach lane from signs and markings.
Distinguish the usual priority rule from a controlled entry.
Check the vehicle ahead before moving.

sections.title: Read the layout before the give-way line
paragraphs: A roundabout is a sequence of decisions, not a single glance to the right. First identify your exit, then read the approach signs, lane arrows and any signals. Choose your lane early enough to avoid a last-second swerve. If local markings differ from a familiar layout, use the information at this junction rather than a memorised lane rule. A navigation instruction helps you choose a destination; it does not override road markings.

Use your mirrors before changing speed or position. Reduce speed to give yourself time to assess the entry and select a suitable gear. Your approach should leave you able to stop smoothly when there is no safe opportunity to join. A vehicle behind you does not make a doubtful gap suitable.

sections.title: Check the entry and the traffic around it
paragraphs: At an ordinary entry, give priority to traffic approaching from the right unless signs, markings or traffic lights direct otherwise. Observe vehicles already circulating, including ones with unclear signals. An indicator is a useful clue, but compare it with the vehicle’s position and movement. Do not enter simply because a driver appears to be signalling to leave.

Keep alternating your view between the circulating traffic and the space immediately ahead. The driver in front may begin to move and then stop. If you keep looking right while your own car rolls forward, you can run into that vehicle even though you correctly identified a gap.

sections.title: Use clear signals for the first exit
paragraphs: For the first exit to the left, the usual approach is the left-hand lane with a left signal, unless signs or markings specify another arrangement. Keep an appropriate left position as you circulate and continue the signal to leave. Signal timing should help others understand your actual route, not suggest you are turning into an earlier entrance.

scenario.title: Work through the situation
scenario.text: You are behind a car at a small roundabout. It rolls forward while you look right, but you then see its brake lights. Keep your own car stopped and reassess both views. When the space ahead is clear and a suitable entry opportunity exists, make a final forward check before moving. The apparent gap on the roundabout was only one part of the decision.

takeaways: Read the exit, lane guidance and controls early.
Judge movements as well as indicators.
A final forward check prevents a common queue collision.

entries.title: Circulating, leaving and sharing the roundabout

lesson.title: Circulating, leaving and sharing the roundabout
objectives: Time exit signals and lane changes safely.
Allow for cyclists, horses and long vehicles.
Apply the normal approach to mini-roundabouts.

sections.title: Prepare to leave without cutting across someone
paragraphs: For an exit to the right, or a full circuit, the usual approach is a right signal and the right-hand lane unless local guidance says otherwise. Keep that position until you need to change lanes for your exit. For an intermediate exit, choose the appropriate approach lane and normally give no approach signal. In both cases, signal left after passing the exit before yours.

A left signal does not create a clear route across another lane. Check mirrors and the area beside you before changing course. Follow the road’s lane guidance and leave only when you can do so safely. If a planned move would force another road user to brake or swerve, continue safely and find another route rather than forcing the exit.

sections.title: Expect other road users to take different paths
paragraphs: Cyclists, horse riders and horse-drawn vehicles may remain in the left-hand lane while continuing around the roundabout. Do not assume that their lane position means they will take the next exit. Give cyclists priority, allow room for their route and do not overtake them within their lane. A right signal from a rider may indicate that they are continuing around.

Long vehicles can need more than one lane to negotiate the curve. Stay out of the narrowing space beside them. Also check the approach and exit roads for people crossing. Give way to people crossing the exit road, and be ready to stop rather than concentrating only on circulating vehicles.

sections.title: Treat each mini-roundabout as its own decision
paragraphs: A painted central circle is still a roundabout. Most vehicles must pass around its markings; the exception is a large vehicle physically unable to do so. Space is limited, so plan early and avoid a U-turn. At a pair or series of mini-roundabouts, reassess priority and traffic separately at each one. Getting through the first does not settle the second.

scenario.title: Work through the situation
scenario.text: You intend to leave at the third exit. A cyclist in the left lane continues beyond the second exit while a lorry occupies extra space ahead. Do not squeeze between them or turn across the cyclist. Keep a safe position, observe their movements, and leave only when your path is clear. Follow the lane guidance and take a safe alternative route if that exit cannot be taken without a conflict.

takeaways: Check the lane beside you before leaving.
Left-lane riders may be continuing around.
Reassess every mini-roundabout separately.

entries.title: Deciding whether an overtake is worth starting

lesson.title: Deciding whether an overtake is worth starting
objectives: Check the complete route past a slower vehicle.
Recognise locations where an overtake is unsafe or prohibited.
Respond safely when another driver passes you.

sections.title: Plan the complete manoeuvre
paragraphs: Before an overtake, identify both the space for moving out and the space for returning. You need enough clear road ahead, a suitable gap beyond the vehicle you will pass, and a check that someone behind is not already overtaking you. Use mirrors and any necessary blind-spot observation before moving. An empty patch beside your car is not proof that the whole manoeuvre can be completed.

Following a lorry too closely reduces your view and makes the decision harder. Increase your separation so that you can see more of the road ahead. Remember that a long vehicle takes more time and distance to pass. Another car’s successful overtake does not reserve a second opportunity for you.

sections.title: Recognise a clear reason to wait
paragraphs: Do not attempt an overtake when a bend, hill crest or other obstruction prevents a clear assessment of the road ahead. A narrowing road or a nearby junction can create a conflict before you have returned safely. Where a no-overtaking sign applies, do not overtake until the restriction is cancelled. Observe the relevant road markings too. A straight stretch alone is not permission to disregard them.

When a parked vehicle or another obstruction is on your side, give way to approaching traffic before moving around it. Waiting behind the obstruction can be the complete, correct plan. Avoid committing yourself to a position that depends on the oncoming driver rescuing the situation.

sections.title: Make room for other people’s decisions
paragraphs: When someone overtakes you, keep a steady course and do not accelerate to compete. If they move into your following space, rebuild a safe gap without an aggressive response. Drivers of slow vehicles should consider a safe opportunity to let a queue pass, rather than holding traffic unnecessarily. Cooperation does not require a sudden stop or an unsafe pull-in.

scenario.title: Work through the situation
scenario.text: A car ahead pulls out to pass a tractor near the brow of a hill. From your position you cannot see a return gap beyond the tractor. Stay back instead of following the car out. It may use the only available space, meet approaching traffic or abandon its own attempt. Your independent view must justify your manoeuvre; its movement cannot do that for you.

takeaways: Check the road ahead, behind and beyond the slower vehicle.
An uncertain view is a reason to wait.
Never turn another driver’s overtake into a race.
