entries.title: Giving people enough room when you pass

lesson.title: Giving people enough room when you pass
objectives: Use the Highway Code clearance guidance.
Explain when to wait instead of passing.
Avoid passing conflicts at turns and crossings.

sections.title: Plan speed and sideways clearance together
paragraphs: A person on a cycle or horse, or walking in the carriageway, has little protection if a vehicle passes too closely. Treat the space beside them as part of your overtaking plan. At speeds up to 30 mph, the Highway Code gives at least 1.5 metres as guidance for passing a cyclist; allow more room at higher speeds. That distance is not a target that makes every pass safe in every condition.

Pass a horse rider or horse-drawn vehicle below 10 mph, allowing at least 2 metres. For someone walking in the road, keep your speed low and allow at least 2 metres. Allow extra space in bad weather or darkness. If the road and approaching traffic do not let you provide suitable clearance, wait behind. Do not turn the guidance into an excuse to force a gap.

sections.title: Understand why a rider may change position
paragraphs: A cyclist may use the centre of a narrow lane or move out to avoid a drain, pothole or parked vehicle. Riding two abreast can help a group’s safety and visibility. A shoulder check may be an early clue that a rider intends to change direction. Leave time for that movement rather than accelerating into the space they need.

Before turning left, do not overtake a cyclist travelling straight ahead and then cut across them. The delay you avoid would come at the cost of a serious conflict. Likewise, do not pass the nearest vehicle stopped to let someone use a pedestrian crossing: the person may be hidden in front of it.

sections.title: Complete the pass without another conflict
paragraphs: When an opportunity becomes suitable, make the manoeuvre deliberately and within the speed limit. Return to your normal road position only after there is enough separation from the person you passed. Avoid sharp steering or acceleration near a horse, and be ready to wait longer if the rider signals for you to slow down or stop.

scenario.title: Work through the situation
scenario.text: You follow a cyclist past parked cars while a vehicle approaches from the opposite direction. There is not enough road width for your car to pass with suitable clearance. Hold back at a safe following distance. When the oncoming vehicle has passed, reassess the complete route and the cyclist’s position. Waiting has created a safer opportunity; it has not made an immediate overtake compulsory.

takeaways: Clearance and low speed both matter.
Wait when there is not enough room.
Never pass a cyclist merely to turn across their route.

entries.title: Reading zebra and parallel crossings

lesson.title: Reading zebra and parallel crossings
objectives: Identify the responsibilities for waiting and crossing users.
Keep crossing approaches and the crossing itself clear.
Explain why a wave is not a safe invitation.

sections.title: Look for people on both sides
paragraphs: A crossing is a place where someone’s route may intersect yours within seconds. Scan the pavement on both sides as well as the stripes ahead. Reduce speed early enough to stop smoothly. A parked van, a queue or darkness may conceal someone approaching the crossing. Treat a blocked view as a reason for extra care, not as evidence that no one is there.

The zig-zag area helps protect visibility around the crossing. You must not park on the crossing or within its zig-zag markings. You must not overtake the moving vehicle nearest the crossing, or the nearest vehicle stopped to give way. Passing it can put you directly into the path of a person you could not previously see.

sections.title: Distinguish waiting from crossing
paragraphs: At a zebra crossing you should give way to a person waiting to cross; once a pedestrian has entered the crossing, giving way is a legal requirement. A parallel crossing adds a cycle route alongside the pedestrian stripes. Apply the corresponding waiting and crossing responsibilities to both pedestrians and cyclists there.

Your own stopped car does not make the opposite lane safe. Do not wave, flash headlights or sound the horn to invite someone across. They must assess the whole road, including vehicles you may not see. Let an older or disabled person finish at their own pace, without edging towards them.

sections.title: Leave a usable path through the crossing
paragraphs: In a queue, wait before the crossing unless you can clear it completely. Stopping across it forces people into an awkward route between vehicles. A zebra or parallel crossing divided by a central island is treated as two crossings. This does not remove the need to observe people approaching either part, and it must not be confused with the different rule for a straight-through pelican crossing.

scenario.title: Work through the situation
scenario.text: A delivery van partly hides the far end of a zebra crossing. The car ahead stops, but you cannot yet see why. Stay behind it and prepare to stop rather than using the empty lane to pass. A pedestrian then appears from in front of the van. After that person finishes, check both approaches again before moving; another person may already be about to use the crossing.

takeaways: Look beyond the crossing surface to both pavements.
Do not overtake a vehicle nearest a crossing.
Leave crossing space clear in queues.

entries.title: Understanding signals and central islands

lesson.title: Understanding signals and central islands
objectives: Apply the pelican flashing-amber rule correctly.
Give way to anyone still crossing when your light changes.
Recognise crossing types with different signal sequences.

sections.title: Observe people as well as the light
paragraphs: At a signal-controlled crossing, read the vehicle signal and the physical situation together. Red requires you to stop at the line. A green signal permits movement only when the route is clear; it is not an instruction to drive at someone still crossing. Keep checking the full crossing area before releasing the brake and moving.

The first vehicle in a queue has a particularly important final observation to make. Drivers behind may be responding to its movement rather than seeing the pedestrian for themselves. Move off deliberately after the crossing is clear, rather than letting pressure from behind decide when you start.

sections.title: Use flashing amber only where it exists
paragraphs: A pelican crossing has a flashing-amber stage after red. During flashing amber, you must give way to any pedestrian still on the crossing. If no one remains on it, you may proceed cautiously. The permission is conditional on what you can actually see. A person screened by another vehicle has not become safe to ignore.

Puffin, toucan and equestrian crossings do not use that flashing-amber stage. Their vehicle lights follow the ordinary traffic-light sequence. A toucan accommodates people cycling as well as walking, so watch for both. Avoid making decisions from the crossing’s nickname alone; follow its actual signals and markings.

sections.title: Check whether the island divides the crossing
paragraphs: A pelican crossing that runs straight across the road is one crossing even when it has a central island. You must wait for pedestrians coming from its other side. This differs from a zebra crossing split by an island. At every crossing, give way to someone still crossing after your signal becomes green. If signals are not working, approach with extreme caution, and do not enter unless you can clear the crossing completely.

scenario.title: Work through the situation
scenario.text: At a straight-through pelican crossing, your signal begins flashing amber. A person has reached the island from the opposite side and continues across. Remain stopped: the island has not created a separate crossing that lets you move first. When that person has finished and you can see the crossing is clear, proceed cautiously if flashing amber remains. At a puffin crossing, do not wait for a flashing-amber stage that will never appear.

takeaways: Flashing amber is a conditional pelican stage.
A green light does not cancel a person’s crossing.
A straight-through pelican remains one crossing across an island.

entries.title: Anticipating people whose needs are easy to miss

lesson.title: Anticipating people whose needs are easy to miss
objectives: Apply greater responsibility without assuming other people will act predictably.
Recognise circumstances needing extra time and observation.
Give riders, children and pedestrians room to act safely.

sections.title: Build a picture beyond the car in front
paragraphs: A car’s size and speed mean its driver can cause substantial harm. The hierarchy of road users asks those able to cause the greatest harm to take greater care; it does not remove anyone else’s responsibility. Use that principle before a conflict develops. In a shopping street, scan gaps between parked cars and around stopped buses. A child concentrating on a friend or an ice-cream van may not be watching traffic.

Before crossing a pavement or cycle route to reach a driveway, give way to pedestrians using the pavement and cyclists using the cycle lane or track. When reversing, inspect the area all around, including the space a turning front corner will sweep through. Do not assume that a person who was visible a moment ago remains clear of the vehicle.

sections.title: Make allowance without demanding a response
paragraphs: Someone’s sight, hearing or mobility needs may not be obvious. An older pedestrian or someone using a walking aid may require extra time to cross. Do not hurry them with the car’s position or engine noise. A white cane with a red band may indicate deafblindness; a horn or hand gesture may not be understood.

Near schools and playgrounds, search for children. Flashing amber lights below a school warning sign call for very slow driving until clear of the area. A stopped school bus is another cue to look for children. A school crossing patrol displaying its stop sign requires you to stop. Look beyond the sign bearer for people still crossing, rather than treating the sign as the only hazard.

sections.title: Make space for riders and animals
paragraphs: Cyclists can use the centre of a narrow lane and may ride two abreast for safety. A glance over a shoulder can precede a change of position. Check for cycles and motorcycles filtering beside slow traffic before turning across it. Pass horses calmly, below 10 mph and with at least 2 metres of clearance when safe; otherwise wait. When animals block a road, be prepared to stop; if a herd blocks it, stop and switch off the engine until it clears. Noise and impatience can make their movement harder to predict.

scenario.title: Work through the situation
scenario.text: You are waiting to turn right through a gap in a slow-moving queue. A driver waves you across, but the queue hides the route beside it. Do not accept the wave as proof of safety. Check for a filtering cyclist or motorcycle and for pedestrians crossing the side road. Wait until you can assess the whole route, then make the turn without forcing another person to change course.

takeaways: Scan the spaces where people may emerge.
Allow additional time without intimidation.
A helpful wave cannot replace your own observation.

sources.title: Highway Code: people requiring extra care, Rules 204–218

entries.title: Sharing with buses, large vehicles and emergency traffic

lesson.title: Sharing with buses, large vehicles and emergency traffic
objectives: Allow for large-vehicle blind spots and turning paths.
Respond calmly to emergency vehicles while obeying controls.
Anticipate quiet, slow and special vehicles.

sections.title: Leave room for size and limited visibility
paragraphs: A large vehicle may need to start a turn farther from the kerb or occupy extra road width as it turns. Do not enter the gap beside it merely because that space looks temporarily empty. Its path can narrow that gap as the turn develops, and its driver may not be able to see your car.

Increase your following separation behind a lorry or coach when its body blocks your view. More distance gives you a better picture of junctions, hazards and possible stopping points ahead. Be patient with a lower travelling speed: many large vehicles have different speed limits or a speed limiter. The speed allowed for your car does not tell you what that vehicle is permitted or able to do.

sections.title: Recognise vehicles with different movement patterns
paragraphs: Give buses, coaches and trams priority when you can do so safely, particularly when they signal to leave a stop. Check for passengers who may cross nearby. A tram cannot steer away from a conflict, and quiet electric movement may be difficult to detect by sound alone. Observe the track and route rather than relying on engine noise.

A flashing amber beacon can warn of a slow or stationary vehicle, recovery work or a large load. Reduce speed and find out what space is available before passing. A small mobility vehicle may not show an amber beacon on an ordinary road; absence of a flashing light is not evidence that everything ahead is travelling at normal traffic speed.

sections.title: Help emergency traffic without another danger
paragraphs: When an emergency vehicle approaches, assess its likely route and make room calmly where safe. Its presence does not itself authorise you to cross a red light or mount the pavement. Avoid harsh braking or stopping where a bend, crest or narrow section creates a fresh hazard. Check mirrors and surroundings before pulling aside; the emergency driver may already have chosen a route around you.

scenario.title: Work through the situation
scenario.text: You are first at a red signal when an ambulance approaches from behind. Keep behind the stop line rather than entering the junction just to create space. Observe its position and the surrounding traffic. When lawful and safe movement becomes possible, make space deliberately without cutting across someone else. Helping means reducing the overall risk, not transferring it to pedestrians or crossing traffic.

takeaways: A temporary gap beside a turning lorry can disappear.
Use distance to improve a blocked view.
Emergency traffic still needs your calm, lawful response.

entries.title: Joining and leaving a motorway

lesson.title: Joining and leaving a motorway
objectives: Join without forcing existing traffic to change course.
Recognise an added lane and plan an exit early.
Recover safely after missing a junction.

sections.title: Prepare before the slip road
paragraphs: Motorway traffic can close a gap much faster than it appears to from a side road. Plan your route before setting off so that lane decisions do not compete with reading a map. A learner car driver may use a motorway only with an approved driving instructor in a dual-controlled car displaying red L plates, or D plates in Wales. Once on the slip road, look well ahead and use mirrors to build a picture of the left lane, rather than staring at one vehicle. Adjust speed to fit a safe gap while staying within the limit.

sections.title: Join the flow, not a race
paragraphs: Traffic already on the motorway has priority. A signal tells other drivers what you intend; it does not reserve a gap or require them to move aside. Keep checking the gap as it develops, including any blind area relevant to a sideways move. Do not cross solid white lines or treat the hard shoulder as an extension of the slip road. If your slip road becomes an extra motorway lane, normally remain in that lane instead of making an unnecessary immediate lane change.

sections.title: Leave with time and space
paragraphs: After joining, remain in the left lane long enough to settle into the traffic before considering an overtake. For an exit, read the signs early, get into the appropriate lane in good time and signal your intention. Reduce speed on the slip road as required by its shape and signs; a motorway cruising speed can feel deceptively slow after a long journey. If you miss the exit, continue to the next junction. Never reverse, cross the central reservation or turn back against the traffic flow.

scenario.title: Put it into practice
scenario.text: Your planned exit appears while you are overtaking two vehicles. There is no safe gap back to the left before the exit. Continue safely past the junction and re-plan at the next exit. Losing a few minutes is preferable to cutting across lanes at the last moment.

takeaways: Existing motorway traffic has priority.
An added lane does not require an immediate merge.
A missed exit means continuing to the next one.

entries.title: Lane discipline and motorway signals

lesson.title: Lane discipline and motorway signals
objectives: Choose lanes according to the task, not their apparent speed.
Respond correctly to warnings, mandatory limits and red X closures.
Check safely before changing lanes.

sections.title: Use the left lane as the normal lane
paragraphs: The motorway's lanes are not divided into slow drivers and fast drivers. Keep left unless overtaking, then return left when it is safe. Before moving, use mirrors, assess traffic ahead and behind, and check any blind area that could hide a vehicle. Give a useful signal and move smoothly into a genuine gap. Leaving a safe following distance still matters while overtaking. A vehicle towing a trailer must not normally use the right-hand lane of a motorway with three or more lanes.

sections.title: Treat information as an early warning
paragraphs: Motorway signs may warn of a hazard that is still beyond your view. Amber flashing signals are a reason to reduce speed and prepare for what lies ahead, not to wait until the obstruction becomes visible. A speed limit shown inside a red circle is compulsory. Follow advance instructions before a lane closure so that you can change lanes safely rather than braking or swerving beneath the final sign. The presence of a warning does not remove your responsibility to choose an appropriate speed for the actual conditions.

sections.title: A closed lane is not spare road space
paragraphs: A red X with flashing red lights means the lane is closed. Do not drive in it; hazards and people may be present even if the first stretch looks empty. Emergency services may also need that lane to reach an incident. A closure of the left lane at an exit can make that exit unavailable. In congestion, stay in your lane when queues are moving at different speeds; do not weave between lanes to gain a few car lengths. Reassess every move rather than following another driver through a restriction.

scenario.title: Put it into practice
scenario.text: You are approaching a red X over the left lane and your satnav says to use that lane for the next exit. Follow the motorway signs and move safely to an open lane. Let the route change rather than entering a closed lane because a navigation instruction is inconvenient.

takeaways: Keep left except when overtaking.
Red-circle speed limits and red X closures must be obeyed.
Plan lane changes early and check the blind area.

entries.title: Stopping, fatigue and motorway emergencies

lesson.title: Stopping, fatigue and motorway emergencies
objectives: Distinguish a rest stop from an emergency stop.
Choose a place of relative safety.
Explain what to do when safe exit is impossible.

sections.title: Stop for the right reason in the right place
paragraphs: Motorway monotony can make you sleepy even when traffic is light. Plan breaks and use a service area or leave at an exit if you need rest. A hard shoulder or emergency area is not a place for a telephone call, a route check or a short sleep. Do not use a hard shoulder as an extra running lane unless the signs permit it. If a problem develops but the vehicle can continue safely, aim for the next service area or leave the motorway rather than stopping beside fast traffic.

sections.title: Go left, then get safe
paragraphs: If continuing is not possible, move left and use an emergency area or hard shoulder if you can. Stop as far left as possible, turn the wheels left and switch on hazard warning lights. Use sidelights if darkness or poor visibility requires them. If it is safe and possible, leave by the side away from traffic and move well away from the vehicle and carriageway, behind a safety barrier where available. Check the ground beyond a barrier for drops or other hazards. Keep passengers together and children under control.

sections.title: Get help without creating another emergency
paragraphs: If you cannot reach relative safety and cannot leave the vehicle safely, stay inside with seat belts and hazard lights on and call 999 for the police, or use the vehicle's SOS button. Explain your location and direction of travel. Do not attempt roadside repairs on a motorway or walk into a live lane to retrieve an object. Never place a warning triangle on a motorway. From an emergency area, use its emergency telephone and follow the operator's instructions before attempting to rejoin; a lane may need to be closed first.

scenario.title: Put it into practice
scenario.text: An engine warning appears just before a service-area entrance. The car can still be driven safely. Use the service area rather than stopping on the hard shoulder. If the car instead loses power in a live lane and no safe exit is possible, keep belts on, use hazards and summon urgent help.

takeaways: Use services for rest; emergency areas are for emergencies.
Stay away from moving traffic if safe exit is possible.
If safe exit is impossible, stay belted and call 999.

entries.title: Rain, grip and following space

lesson.title: Rain, grip and following space
objectives: Explain how wet weather changes stopping and observation.
Choose a suitable following gap.
Respond smoothly when tyres lose contact with the road.

sections.title: Plan for less grip and a poorer view
paragraphs: A wet road gives the tyres less grip, so the distance needed to stop is at least double the dry-road distance. Rain and spray can also hide the hazard that would make you brake. Reduce speed to suit the view and leave enough space to see past the vehicle ahead. Take extra care near pedestrians, cyclists and motorcyclists, whose position or stability may change around water. After a long dry spell, the first rain can make the surface particularly slippery; familiar roads still need a fresh assessment.

sections.title: Use time, then increase it for conditions
paragraphs: At high speed, a dry-road following gap should be at least two seconds. Choose a fixed roadside feature, note when the vehicle ahead passes it, and count until your own vehicle reaches it. On a wet road, at least double that gap. Four seconds is therefore a minimum starting point in wet high-speed conditions, not a promise that every speed and surface is safe. Increase the space further when visibility or grip is worse. Dropping back also improves the chance of seeing a brake-light warning early.

sections.title: Avoid sudden reactions to surface water
paragraphs: If steering becomes unusually light or unresponsive in heavy rain, water may be preventing the tyres from gripping the road. Ease off the accelerator and slow gradually rather than making an abrupt steering or braking input. Look well ahead so that reducing speed happens before deep water or a bend whenever possible. A shiny diesel spill can be extremely slippery, especially when wet. Do not assume that a large vehicle ahead will uncover every hazard for you; its spray can make following closely both less visible and less controllable.

scenario.title: Put it into practice
scenario.text: A van ahead throws spray over your windscreen. Instead of staying close to use its tail-lights as a guide, increase the gap and reduce speed until you can see enough clear road. If the van brakes suddenly, the extra space gives you time to react and stop.

takeaways: Wet stopping distances are at least double dry distances.
At least double the two-second high-speed gap in rain.
Ease off smoothly if steering loses response in water.

entries.title: Fog, wind and bright weather

lesson.title: Fog, wind and bright weather
objectives: Choose lights that help without dazzling others.
Anticipate sudden changes in wind and visibility.
Respond safely to glare and heat-related fatigue.

sections.title: Drive within the view you actually have
paragraphs: Before entering fog, check mirrors and reduce speed. A clear patch after a fog warning does not mean the whole route has cleared; another bank may appear suddenly. Keep a gap that allows you to stop within the distance you can see is clear. Do not simply follow the red lights ahead, because their apparent visibility can encourage an unsafe speed or gap. Use wipers and demisters to keep the windscreen clear. If another driver follows too closely, do not accelerate into a view you cannot safely use.

sections.title: Use lights for conditions, then change them back
paragraphs: When visibility is seriously reduced, generally when you cannot see beyond 100 metres, headlights must be used. Front or rear fog lights may also be used in those conditions, but must be switched off when visibility improves. Unnecessary fog lights can dazzle and make brake lights harder to distinguish. At a junction in fog, stop correctly, look and listen carefully before emerging. Once you know it is safe, move positively without stopping where you would block the path of approaching traffic. Lighting is an aid to observation, not a substitute for it.

sections.title: Expect movement you cannot predict exactly
paragraphs: Crosswinds can push a car or vulnerable road user sideways. Be especially prepared on exposed bridges, open stretches and gaps in hedges. Passing a large vehicle may change the wind pressure around you, and a motorcyclist can be especially affected by that turbulence. Give space rather than trying to pass closely. In hot weather, ventilation can improve comfort but does not cure tiredness: arrange a safe rest stop if you become sleepy. If low sun dazzles you, reduce speed and, if necessary, stop safely rather than driving without an adequate view.

scenario.title: Put it into practice
scenario.text: A fog bank clears as you reach an exposed bridge. Reassess both problems: switch off unnecessary fog lights, but keep enough space for the gusts that may affect you or the motorcyclist ahead. Better visibility does not remove the separate risk from wind.

takeaways: Use headlights in seriously reduced visibility.
Switch fog lights off when the conditions improve.
Allow extra room for gusts, glare and unstable road users.

entries.title: Preparing for snow and ice

lesson.title: Preparing for snow and ice
objectives: Decide whether a winter journey is necessary.
Clear the vehicle properly before departure.
Prepare for delays and changing route conditions.

sections.title: Decide before the car moves
paragraphs: Snow and ice can make a normally simple journey difficult to control or complete. Check local forecasts and travel warnings rather than judging only the road outside your home. The Highway Code advises against driving in these conditions unless the journey is essential. If it is essential, allow more time, consider the route and identify safer alternatives or stopping places. A time commitment does not make an unsafe journey necessary; changing an appointment may be the safer decision. Tell someone your plan when there is a realistic chance of becoming stranded.

sections.title: Clear more than a small viewing hole
paragraphs: You must be able to see, so remove snow and ice from every window, not just a patch in front of the steering wheel. Clear mirrors and demist the inside of the glass thoroughly. Lights must be clean and number plates visible and legible. Remove snow that could fall from the vehicle into the path of other road users, including snow on the roof that might slide across your own view when braking. Complete these jobs while parked safely, before expecting the ventilation or wipers to solve them on the move.

sections.title: Carry help and keep checking the plan
paragraphs: For an essential winter journey, take items that help if you are delayed: de-icer and scraper, warm clothing and boots, a torch, first-aid kit, jump leads and a shovel, with food and a warm drink. Prepare the vehicle for the conditions rather than relying only on an emergency bag. Check that the intended route is not already blocked and that more severe weather is not forecast. Once travelling, listen to travel information and variable signs. Conditions may change over a short distance, so be willing to stop safely or revise the plan.

scenario.title: Put it into practice
scenario.text: You have cleared the windscreen but the side windows, lights and roof remain covered. The destination is only a mile away. Finish clearing the vehicle before departure, then reassess whether the journey is essential. A short distance still requires visibility and must not shed a hazard behind you.

takeaways: Avoid non-essential journeys in snow or ice.
Clear windows, mirrors, lights, plates and loose roof snow.
Prepare for delays and reassess the route.

entries.title: Maintaining control on ice

lesson.title: Maintaining control on ice
objectives: Explain why stopping space must grow greatly.
Use gentle inputs before bends and when starting.
Recognise that treatment does not guarantee grip.

sections.title: Leave room for a much longer stop
paragraphs: Ice can reduce grip so much that stopping distances may be ten times the dry-road distance. Leave a very large gap rather than copying the distance used by a driver ahead. Drive carefully even where a road has been treated: gritting is not a guarantee that every shaded patch, bridge or junction is clear. Conditions can vary within a short stretch, and information signs may warn of hazards you have not reached. Reduce demands on the tyres before the difficult surface rather than waiting for the car to slide.

sections.title: Make acceleration, braking and steering gentle
paragraphs: Avoid sudden actions, because a tyre needs grip to change speed or direction. In a manual car, use a suitably high gear at a slow, safe speed and accelerate gently to reduce the chance of wheelspin. Before a bend, brake progressively while travelling straight, then steer smoothly around it at the reduced speed. Do not brake hard only after entering the bend. Vehicle controls and transmission instructions vary, so use the manufacturer's advice alongside the general principle of avoiding sharp changes in force. Extra technology cannot create grip where the surface provides very little.

sections.title: Observe the surface and the vehicles treating it
paragraphs: Very little tyre noise can be a clue that the road is icy. If you are uncertain about grip, only test it by gentle braking in a safe place where that action will not put anyone at risk. A winter maintenance vehicle may be spreading salt or throwing snow into adjoining space, so keep clear and be cautious around it. Do not pass a snowplough unless the lane you intend to use has been cleared. Progress is secondary to having a safe path, a useful view and enough stopping room.

scenario.title: Put it into practice
scenario.text: A gritted main road leads into a shaded bend and the tyre noise becomes unusually quiet. Ease speed down on the straight, keep a much larger following gap and steer gently. Do not interpret the earlier grit treatment as permission to keep the same speed through a potentially icy bend.

takeaways: Stopping on ice may require ten times the dry-road distance.
Slow before bends and avoid sudden controls.
Treated roads and snow-clearing vehicles still need caution.

entries.title: Reading parking restrictions

lesson.title: Reading parking restrictions
objectives: Distinguish waiting restrictions from stopping restrictions.
Read zone signs, markings and reserved bays together.
Keep crossings, junctions and access routes usable.

sections.title: Read the whole restriction
paragraphs: Yellow lines control waiting, and their operating times come from nearby plates or the signs at a Controlled Parking Zone entrance. Double yellow lines mean no waiting at any time even without a separate upright sign. A stopping restriction is stricter than a waiting restriction: do not assume that remaining in the driver's seat makes a brief stop acceptable. Clearways and signed school entrance markings require particular attention. Look for the complete combination of lines, signs and local conditions before deciding where a passenger can get out or a delivery can be made.

sections.title: Use bays only for their stated purpose
paragraphs: A marked parking place may have conditions concerning time, payment or eligible users. A Blue Badge bay is reserved for those entitled to use it; a vacant bay is not general permission. Controlled-zone entry signs can supply the usual waiting times, while particular bays may have their own instructions. Do not park in an operating tram lane that is not available to your vehicle. In London and Scotland, pavement parking is prohibited, with exceptions only in limited circumstances. Elsewhere, you should not park on the pavement unless signs permit it. Pavement parking can obstruct wheelchair users, people with visual impairments and people with pushchairs.

sections.title: Think about the space others need
paragraphs: A space can be physically large enough for your car but still unsafe or unlawful to use. Keep the zig-zag approaches to pedestrian crossings clear. Do not stop or park opposite or within 10 metres of a junction unless in an authorised parking space. Do not obstruct emergency access, a fire-station entrance or an entrance that others need to use. Look beyond the length of your own car: a wheelchair user, an emergency vehicle or a driver emerging from a junction may need the space you would remove. Choose an off-street parking area or a suitable marked bay wherever possible.

scenario.title: Put it into practice
scenario.text: There is a car-sized gap beside double yellow lines near a junction. A passenger says you can wait there because you will remain in the vehicle. Check the restriction and the junction position; staying at the wheel does not turn waiting into unrestricted parking. Choose a lawful place that preserves visibility and access.

takeaways: Check signs and markings together, including zone entry signs.
A free space is not automatically a permitted space.
Keep crossings, junctions and emergency access clear.

entries.title: Leaving a parked vehicle safely

lesson.title: Leaving a parked vehicle safely
objectives: Secure a parked car and protect passing road users.
Check the night-parking lighting rules.
Avoid hazards caused by doors, passengers or charging leads.

sections.title: Complete the stop before leaving
paragraphs: Roadside parking should normally face with the traffic flow and be close to the side. Before leaving, switch off the engine, headlights and fog lights and apply the parking brake. Make the vehicle secure and put valuables out of sight. On a hill, combine the parking brake with the appropriate gear and wheel position: uphill, a forward gear and wheels away from the kerb; downhill, reverse and wheels towards the kerb. Use Park for an automatic. Follow the vehicle's instructions for its controls rather than assuming the parking brake alone completes every situation.

sections.title: Doors and passengers create moving hazards
paragraphs: You must not hit another road user when opening a door. Check all around, including mirrors and the view over your shoulder, for cyclists and other traffic. Where possible, using the hand farther from the door encourages the body to turn and improves that shoulder check. Passengers, especially children, are generally safer leaving on the kerb side. Do not place the car so close to a Blue Badge vehicle that its occupants lose needed space. At an electric charger, keep cables from becoming a trip hazard and replace them neatly when finished.

sections.title: A parked car must still be visible
paragraphs: At night, do not park facing against traffic unless in a recognised parking space. Parking lights are required on a road or lay-by where the speed limit is greater than 30 mph. Some vehicles, including ordinary cars, can be parked without lights on roads limited to 30 mph or less only under the conditions in the Code, such as a recognised parking place or being close to the kerb, facing with traffic and at least 10 metres from a junction. Do not apply that exception to every vehicle or projecting load. Parking on a road in fog is particularly hazardous; if unavoidable, leave parking lights or sidelights on.

scenario.title: Put it into practice
scenario.text: You park after dark on a 40 mph road. Switching off the headlights does not remove the requirement for parking lights. After securing the car, check the lighting rule and look for passing cyclists before opening the door. Ask a child passenger to leave on the kerb side.

takeaways: Secure the vehicle and use the correct parking procedure.
Check before opening any door.
Night parking has direction and lighting requirements.

entries.title: Responding to a breakdown

lesson.title: Responding to a breakdown
objectives: Choose a safer stopping place before calling recovery.
Explain the safe-exit and unsafe-exit responses.
Give useful location information and avoid dangerous retrieval.

sections.title: Think about relative safety first
paragraphs: When a vehicle develops a problem, the first decision is where people and the vehicle will be least exposed to moving traffic. A service area or another place designed for parking is safer than a hard shoulder beside high-speed traffic. If you can continue safely to an exit or service area, do so. If not, move left towards an emergency area or hard shoulder where possible, stop far left with wheels turned left and use hazard lights. Do not continue driving a vehicle that cannot be controlled safely just to reach a preferred stopping place.

sections.title: Choose the response that is actually safe
paragraphs: If safe and possible, leave on the side away from traffic and get passengers well away from the vehicle and carriageway, behind a barrier where available. Do not stand where the car could be forced into you. If you cannot reach a place of relative safety and cannot exit safely, remain inside with belts and hazards on and call 999 for the police or use the SOS button. A disability may prevent safe exit even where another person could get out. Explain that situation urgently rather than attempting an unsafe transfer into traffic.

sections.title: Help rescuers find you without entering danger
paragraphs: Give the road, direction and location as accurately as possible. Motorway marker posts, driver location signs and an appropriate mapping application can help; quote visible numbers rather than guessing a junction. An emergency telephone can provide assistance, and recovery operators should know if you are a vulnerable motorist. Never place a warning triangle on a motorway or retrieve luggage from a live lane. If an object falls onto a motorway, reach relative safety and call 999. Before leaving an emergency area after recovery, use its telephone and follow the operator's instructions for a safe rejoin.

scenario.title: Put it into practice
scenario.text: A suitcase comes off a roof rack onto a motorway lane. Do not run back to collect it, even if it appears close. Stop in a place of relative safety and call the emergency services with the road, direction and best available location details so traffic can be managed safely.

takeaways: Reach relative safety where possible.
If safe exit is impossible, stay belted and call 999.
Do not retrieve objects or put a triangle on a motorway.

entries.title: At a collision: protect, report and exchange details

lesson.title: At a collision: protect, report and exchange details
objectives: Reduce the risk of a second collision.
Recognise dangerous-goods hazards.
State the duty to stop and provide or report details.

sections.title: Avoid becoming part of the incident
paragraphs: Flashing emergency lights may be the first warning of an incident beyond a bend or over a crest. Reduce speed and be ready to stop or change lane safely. Follow police and traffic-officer directions. Workers, debris and stationary vehicles may occupy space that normally carries traffic. When an incident is on the other carriageway, keep attention on your own road rather than slowing unnecessarily to look. That distraction can create another collision or a queue. Treat every approach as a changing scene and preserve enough room to respond.

sections.title: Protect people without adding hazards
paragraphs: If you are involved or stop to help, use a place of relative safety where possible and warn others with hazard lights. Ask for engines to be switched off and for nobody to smoke. Move uninjured people away from vehicles and moving traffic if that can be done safely. A vehicle marked for dangerous goods may create hazards that are not visible, including flammable material. Keep well away and tell emergency services what markings can be read from a safe place. Do not approach a leaking load or use a mobile phone close to a vehicle carrying flammable goods.

sections.title: Stopping and reporting are separate responsibilities
paragraphs: After a collision causing injury or damage to another person, vehicle, animal or property, you must stop. Give your own and the vehicle owner's name and address and the vehicle registration to someone with reasonable grounds to request them. If required name and address details are not given at the time, report to police as soon as reasonably practicable and within 24 hours. Where another person is injured and the insurance certificate is not produced as required at the scene, the Code also requires police reporting as soon as possible and within 24 hours, and production of the certificate within seven days.

scenario.title: Put it into practice
scenario.text: After a low-speed collision, both drivers can move safely out of the road and nobody appears injured. Do not simply drive away because the damage is small. Stop, exchange the required details and follow reporting requirements if those details cannot be provided. Remain alert to other traffic while dealing with the situation.

takeaways: Approach incidents cautiously and follow official directions.
Keep clear of dangerous goods and prevent smoking.
Stop, exchange required details and report when required.

entries.title: Helping people while emergency services respond

lesson.title: Helping people while emergency services respond
objectives: Put scene safety before approaching a casualty.
Give clear information to an emergency call handler.
Avoid harmful movement and recognise the limits of this lesson.

sections.title: Check danger before giving help
paragraphs: A person needing help can draw attention away from fast traffic, broken glass, spilled fuel or a vehicle that may move. Check that it is safe to approach, and keep yourself and uninjured people away from the path of traffic. If possible, use other bystanders to help without creating a crowd around the casualty. Have someone call 999 or 112 promptly. Give the exact location, direction of travel and number of vehicles, then describe what is actually observed: for example, someone trapped, heavy bleeding, breathing difficulty or no response when spoken to.

sections.title: Do not improvise treatment
paragraphs: Do not normally move an injured person from a vehicle unless there is immediate danger. Do not remove a motorcyclist's helmet unless it is essential and you are trained to do so. Reassure casualties, keep them warm and dry where possible, and do not give food or drink. Stay with them if it is safe, watch for changes and pass those changes to the emergency service. An untrained helper should follow the call handler's instructions, explaining clearly what they can and cannot do rather than guessing at a medical technique.

sections.title: Use training and professional guidance
paragraphs: If someone does not respond, tell the emergency call handler immediately and follow their questions and directions about breathing and urgent care. Do not delay calling because you are trying to diagnose an injury yourself. First-aid skills can make a difference, but a short driving lesson is not a replacement for practical first-aid training. The Highway Code's first-aid annex is a general guide and any help at the roadside is temporary until professional care arrives. Keep your own safety under review throughout: a change in traffic or fire risk may change what assistance is possible.

scenario.title: Put it into practice
scenario.text: A motorcyclist is injured but the immediate position is safe. A bystander proposes taking off the helmet and giving water. Keep the helmet in place unless essential and appropriately trained, give no food or drink, call for emergency help and follow the call handler's guidance while reassuring the casualty.

takeaways: Check danger, summon help and describe observations clearly.
Avoid unnecessary movement, helmet removal, food or drink.
Follow emergency guidance; seek practical first-aid training.
